title: Al-Humazah: the slanderer
hook: woe to the backbiter who counts his money and thinks it will keep him (Surah 104)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Fil, the army of the elephant, and a grandfather who asked for his camels. Your line was the house was defended. Did you do your part and leave the rest? Day one hundred seventy.

Everyone has met this person, and most of us have been him for an afternoon. The one who does impressions of a coworker the moment she leaves the room. The eye-roll across the table. The group chat screenshot with a laughing emoji. It feels small, and it feels safe, especially when you're the one with more money, more status, more followers. Today's surah has a word for this person, and it doesn't treat it as small at all. Nine lines, and it opens with woe. Today: Al-Humazah, the slanderer.
screen: `THE IMPRESSION BEHIND HER BACK.` → `THE EYE-ROLL, THE SCREENSHOT.` → `IT OPENS WITH WOE.`

segments.voice: Surah one hundred four begins, in Pickthall's translation: Woe unto every slandering traducer, Who hath gathered wealth and arrangeth it. He thinketh that his wealth will render him immortal. In Arabic the first line is two sharp words: humazah, lumazah. Commentators give them related shades. One is mocking with gestures, the look, the smirk, the pointed finger. The other is wounding with the tongue, especially behind someone's back. Both are forms of the same thing: making someone smaller so you can feel bigger. And then the surah does something revealing. It moves straight from mockery to money. The mocker is also the man counting his wealth, over and over, arranging it. The two go together. Contempt for people and trust in money come from the same place: the belief that you're safe, above it all, untouchable. He thinks his wealth will make him last forever. The surah says no, and describes a fire that reaches the heart, the place where the contempt began. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gave a plain definition of backbiting, recorded in Sahih Muslim. He asked his companions: do you know what backbiting is? It's mentioning your brother in a way he would dislike. Someone asked: what if it's true? He said: if it's true, that's backbiting. If it's false, that's slander. So the test isn't whether the joke is accurate. It's whether they'd be hurt to hear it. Money won't keep you. Neither will the laugh at someone else's expense.
screen: `HUMAZAH, LUMAZAH — THE LOOK, THE TONGUE.` · `FROM MOCKERY STRAIGHT TO MONEY.` · `HE THINKS HIS WEALTH WILL KEEP HIM.` · `EVEN IF IT'S TRUE, IT'S BACKBITING.` · then, large: `MONEY WON'T KEEP YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and think honestly about the last time you mocked someone, out loud, in a message, or just with a look. No need for guilt; just see it clearly. What were you protecting? Then picture that person hearing it. Let the picture be real for a moment. Now decide: for the rest of today, no mocking. Not in words, not in texts, not with your eyes. The bell holds the time.
Al-Humazah. The slanderer, the one who mocks and belittles; the name of Surah one hundred four. Today's word.
Your line: money won't keep you. Go one day without mocking anyone. When the joke at someone's expense rises up, let it pass unsaid. Day one hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Humazah in the prayers, and Islamic teaching treats backbiting (ghibah) and slander as serious wrongs; many try to leave a gathering or change the subject when others are mocked.

original.note: Arabic: one who mocks and belittles, the first key word of Surah 104.

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah about gossip.
what it means: mockery and trust in money grow from the same false sense of being untouchable.
what a scholar hears: humazah and lumazah are intensive forms (habitual mockers); Muslim 2589 defines ghibah; the fire 'reaching the hearts' (104:7) answers where contempt starts.
